title: Wet-Lab Materials Bill-of-Materials Scanner
one_liner: Black Duck for biology: scan a startup's plasmids, cell lines, antibodies and enzymes for license, MTA and patent encumbrances before an investor or acquirer does.
customer: Venture-backed biotechs 6-12 months from a Series B, IPO or M&A, acquirers' diligence teams, university spinouts, and IP counsel.
problem: Materials used freely in academia carry limits in for-profit use: Addgene third-party limited-use label licenses, research-only cell-line licenses, Cas9, base-editor and promoter patents, and MTA restrictions. Nobody inventories a lab's biological dependencies, so surprises surface in diligence and cut price or delay closing. At least 12 funded biotechs were sold for $1B+ in 2026, so acquirer diligence is intense.
solution: Ingest LIMS or Benchling exports, plasmid GenBank files and strain and cell-line lists. Match them against a curated encumbrance database (Addgene label-license data, depositor MTAs, patent sequence claims, vendor terms). Output a risk-ranked report with remediation options (license, replace, design around), continuous scanning as inventory changes, and attorney-reviewed summaries.
why_now: Deal volume is high, LIMS exports are easy, and software license scanning is a well-understood category that buyers already recognize.
revenue_model: $12-40k per scan, $30-100k annual continuous monitoring, and sprint pricing for acquirers' diligence teams.
non_obvious_insight: In software, license scanning is standard. In biology the dependencies are physical, unlisted and cross borders, so no bill of materials exists. One database sells to both sides: acquirers use it to find hidden liabilities, startups use it to fix them cheaply before the deal.
first_30_days: Build scanner v0 for plasmid sequences against about 200 known encumbered parts and labels. Run free scans for 10 startups through the SynBioBeta network and convert 3 to $12-15k audits. Recruit an IP attorney as advisor.

title: Green-Claims Clearance for EU-Bound Brands
one_liner: A crawl-and-fix service that strips or substantiates banned 'eco-friendly' and 'climate-neutral' claims on packaging, product pages and ads for brands selling into the EU.
customer: DTC brands, Amazon and Shopify sellers, and mid-size consumer-goods companies selling to EU consumers, plus their marketing agencies and EU authorised representatives.
problem: Directive (EU) 2024/825 applies from 27 Sept 2026. It bans generic environmental claims ('green', 'eco-friendly') without recognised excellent performance, bans offset-based 'climate neutral' claims, and restricts sustainability labels to certified or public schemes. Small brands have thousands of SKUs of copy across 24 languages and no clear way to check it.
solution: Crawl product pages, packaging PDFs and ad libraries, flag banned and risky patterns in 24 languages, and suggest compliant rewrites with evidence-pack templates (life-cycle summary, certification proof). Add a human legal-review tier and monitoring of competitors' claims for complaint filing.
why_now: The rule began applying on 27 Sept 2026, and member-state transposition laws are now in force. The separate Green Claims Directive was shelved, so consultancies shifted attention, yet this ban is already law and cheap to police by machine.
revenue_model: $1-5k initial audit, $300-1,500 per month monitoring, and agency white-label licences.
non_obvious_insight: This is a deadline-driven, per-SKU checking problem that suits software plus a thin human legal layer, and the first enforcement will often start with competitor complaints. The best lead-gen is showing a brand its own violations.
first_30_days: Build a claims lexicon in five languages. Scan the top 200 product categories on Amazon.de and .fr for violations. Email brand founders their own violations as a free preview. Partner with three EU marketing agencies.

title: Compliance Co-op for Group-Buy Hobby Hardware
one_liner: A pooled EU compliance desk (CRA incident reporting, EU responsible person, battery/e-waste registrations, SBOM monitoring) that lets one-person keyboard, FPV, synth and LoRa hardware makers keep selling to Europe.
customer: Boutique hardware makers of 1-20 people in enthusiast scenes: custom mechanical keyboards, eurorack/synth modules, FPV drone boards, LoRa/Meshtastic radios, 3D-printer upgrade kits. They sell through group buys, Tindie, Kickstarter and Discord shops, including US and Asian makers shipping into the EU/UK, plus the boutique vendors that resell them.
problem: Per the briefing, the EU Cyber Resilience Act's 24-hour vulnerability/incident reporting duty went live 11 Sep 2026 for products with digital elements, Data Act connected-product design duties began 12 Sep 2026, and full CRA conformity is due 11 Dec 2027 (fines up to EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover). Those duties fall on whoever sells the product, and in hobby scenes that is a hobbyist selling a 300-unit run built on open-source firmware (QMK, Betaflight, Klipper, Meshtastic). The CRA's open-source carve-out protects non-commercial projects, not the person selling hardware with the firmware. Stack on the EU General Product Safety Regulation's EU-responsible-person requirement (in force since Dec 2024), radio-equipment cybersecurity rules, and battery and WEEE registrations (battery labelling duties start around Aug 2026, verify), and the makers' choices are to ignore it or stop shipping to the EU. A EUR 5-10k consultancy engagement is impossible on an $80-300 product.
solution: A membership 'compliance-of-record' co-op. Members get: a named EU responsible person and CRA contact of record (professional-indemnity insured); a shared coordinated-vulnerability-disclosure desk with a tested runbook for filing on ENISA's single reporting platform within 24 hours; a CI plug-in that generates SBOMs and watches firmware dependencies (QMK, ChibiOS, ESP-IDF, Zephyr etc.) for exploited CVEs; declaration-of-conformity and technical-file templates by product class; a battery/EPR registration bundle; and a group-buy contract addendum covering delivery windows and customised-goods withdrawal rights. The co-op also acts as liaison to upstream open-source firmware projects and channels 'sponsored security fixes' to them.
why_now: CRA reporting has been live for about 18 days and the Data Act design duties for 17 (per briefing). Market-surveillance sweeps and marketplace delistings typically follow such dates, and marketplaces already delist listings that lack GPSR data. Full conformity lands 11 Dec 2027, so scenes will look for a shared answer during 2026-27, before any vendor has locked the niche.
revenue_model: Annual dues tiered by EU units shipped (about EUR 390/yr up to 500 units, EUR 1,200 up to 5,000, custom above). Per-SKU onboarding fee of EUR 250-750. Optional micro-levy of EUR 0.10-0.25 per unit that funds the incident desk and upstream firmware maintainers. Paid 'CRA sprint' for makers with more than 5 SKUs.
non_obvious_insight: Regulators wrote these rules for companies with a compliance department, but the enthusiast hardware economy is thousands of micro-manufacturers who share the same three failure points: firmware dependencies, 24-hour incident reporting, and an EU address. The scalable unit of compliance is the scene or firmware ecosystem, not the individual maker. A co-op that pools the boring 80% and is trusted inside the scene's Discords beats both a law firm and a generic authorised-representative vendor, because reputation in the scene is the distribution channel.
first_30_days: Pick one scene (custom keyboards on QMK/VIA, or LoRa/Meshtastic). Interview 15 makers from group-buy vendor lists. Have a compliance lawyer and a firmware engineer write a one-page '24-hour CRA reporting runbook' and post it free in the scene's Discords, r/MechanicalKeyboards and Geekhack. Sign 10 founding members at about EUR 250 for year one, deliver an incident-reporting drill and a template technical file for one product class, and sell fixed-price single-SKU audits. Cost is two part-time experts plus a simple site, and break-even is roughly 40 members.

title: Interim Smoke-Damage Protocol Before the State Standard
one_liner: Publish and run the defensible smoke, ash and soot assessment protocol that California insurers, adjusters and lawyers will need on January 1, 2027, because the official technical standard will not exist until 2028-2029.
customer: California carriers, the FAIR Plan and their TPAs (for AB 1795's 30-day inspection and testing obligations), plus public adjusters, policyholder attorneys, and escrow, lender and buyer parties in standing-home sales. Homeowners pay via their insurer, PA or directly.
problem: California signed AB 1795 and AB 1642 on Sept 15, 2026. From Jan 1, 2027, insurers must inspect within 30 days, pay for necessary testing, keep paying ALE until restoration, and face a presumption that ash, soot and char in a standing home are fire-caused. But the state toxics department will not finish lead and asbestos standards until end of 2028 and other contaminant standards until 2029. Meanwhile tens of thousands of claims will need a protocol that survives litigation; existing vendor assessments are already accused of being substandard, and capacity of qualified industrial hygienists is scarce and expensive.
solution: An independent, openly published interim assessment protocol built on existing standards (IICRC S700, established sampling and lab methods, EPA/HUD dust-wipe criteria), developed with certified industrial hygienists and a toxicologist. Delivered as a product: a sampling-plan generator (which rooms, surfaces and ducts, how many samples), a trained technician network with kits and a chain-of-custody app, remote IH sign-off, a lab partner, a compliance-clock dashboard for carriers, and a 'smoke clearance certificate' for resale and escrow. Priced at a fraction of full CIH scopes.
why_now: The laws were signed two weeks ago with an effective date of Jan 1, 2027, LA County is investigating Farmers over Eaton/Palisades claim denials, a proposed class action targets vendor assessments, and carriers oppose but must comply. The gap between the compliance date and the state standard is a 2-3 year window in which the best-documented protocol becomes the de facto reference, and other fire states (Colorado, Oregon, Hawaii) are watching.
revenue_model: Per-home assessment of $1,800-$4,500 (paid by insurer under AB 1795 or the policyholder), $500 clearance-certificate add-on, lab pass-through margin, SaaS compliance dashboard for carriers at $2-$5 per claim per month, and training and certification fees for restoration technicians.
non_obvious_insight: In smoke disputes the lab is rarely the fight; the fight is the sampling design and the pass/fail threshold. Carriers whose vendors sample five spots and compare against urban background dust get 'clean' results by construction. Whoever publishes a transparent, replicable sampling grid with chain of custody writes the eventual standard, because regulators borrow the protocol with the most field data.
first_30_days: Recruit two CIHs and one toxicologist as an advisory board and draft 'Interim Smoke Assessment Protocol v0.1' for public comment. Train 6-10 IICRC-certified restoration technicians and buy sampling kits. Sell 20 pilot assessments in Altadena and Palisades at a subsidized $950 through public adjusters and attorneys, gathering data and case studies. Pitch 3 carriers and 2 TPAs on 30-day compliance capacity before January 1, offering a pilot at cost in exchange for using the protocol.

title: Referee Pathway: Officiating as a School Credential
one_liner: A semester-long, credit-bearing officiating course that puts teens in mentored cohorts on paid youth games, fixing the referee shortage by fixing retention.
customer: District CTE directors and state high-school athletic associations are the buyers. Youth leagues and game assignors are paying placement partners. Students (14+ where state rules allow) are the beneficiaries.
problem: Youth and high-school games are shortened or cancelled for lack of officials. Widely cited surveys say most new officials quit within two years, largely because of abuse from parents and fans. Meanwhile teens lack decent first jobs, entry-level white-collar hiring has cracked, and districts are chasing CTE pathways that lead to real work.
solution: A CTE elective, 'Officiating and Conflict Management'. Students learn rules, mechanics, film review and de-escalation role-play. They then work mentored, paid assignments as a cohort (never alone) at rec-league games, with body-worn cameras or comms for protection. The output is a portable 'Registered Official' credential aligned with the state association's licensing. We sell curriculum, assignment scheduling and an insurance wrapper.
why_now: The officials shortage has persisted since COVID and many states have passed laws penalizing assault on officials. CTE enrollment is rising (vocational-heavy public two-years grew 11.7% in Spring 2025). After the entry-level AI job shock, schools and parents want credentials tied to human judgment. Sports is one of the few settings where judgment under pressure is the actual job.
revenue_model: $150-300 per student license paid by districts from CTE budgets. An 8-10% platform fee on paid assignments (typically $40-80 per game). State-association sponsorships and body-cam/insurance partner rebates. A 40-student district cohort is roughly $8-12k plus assignment fees.
non_obvious_insight: The shortage is a retention problem caused by isolation and abuse in an official's first 20 games, not a recruiting problem. A school cohort is the only structure that gives new officials a team, a mentor and institutional backing. De-escalating under hostile scrutiny is also a transferable credential for security, hospitality, HR and healthcare jobs.
first_30_days: Pitch 2-3 CTE directors and the local officials' association. Run a 10-12 week after-school pilot for 30 students, funded by a rec league or booster at about $99 per student. Track how many are still officiating a season later against the roughly 20% baseline. Use the retention data and a league letter of support to pitch the state association.

title: Signed Eyewitness Network for Ports and Sanctions
one_liner: A network of ship, plane and port spotters and local creators paid per provenance-signed capture (verified time, place and device), sold first to maritime insurers and sanctions teams and next to Coast Guard, Navy and intelligence analysts.
customer: Sanctions-compliance teams at banks, commodity traders and marine insurers or P&I brokers ($40-150 per verified task, $2-5K/month watchlist subscriptions). Later buyers are Coast Guard, CBP, NGA and defense OSINT analysts through SBIR or commercial solutions openings.
problem: Open-source analysis is bottlenecked on 'who shot this and when', not on analysis. AI fakes and unverified feeds enter analytic workflows: a SOCOM analyst's chatbot fabricated a cargo manifest and aircraft were airborne before the error was caught, while Maven now has 100K+ users and leaders admit gaps in logistics data visibility. Hobbyist spotters and drone and dashcam creators already sit at chokepoints, but their images cannot be trusted, priced or bought.
solution: Buyers post look-and-verify tasks ('is tanker X at berth Y today?'). Spotters reply with C2PA-signed captures from phones with native content credentials (prior knowledge: recent Pixel and Samsung models). The platform validates the signature chain, GNSS and time, and cross-checks sun angle, weather and AIS, then packages an analyst-ready evidence artifact with a spotter reputation score. Buyers purchase a signed artifact, not labor, so this is not a freelancer marketplace.
why_now: Native camera signing shipped on mainstream phones (prior knowledge) and C2PA reached spec 2.3, so no proprietary hardware is needed. Sanctions and shadow-fleet enforcement and the 2026 Iran conflict raise verification demand, and GenAI.mil put AI summarization in front of 2M users, making trusted ground-truth inputs the scarce resource.
revenue_model: Per-task fees with a 30% platform take, watchlist subscriptions, and government contracts later.
non_obvious_insight: AI is making analysis abundant and cheap while trusted ground truth stays scarce. The hobbyist spotter community is an existing, unpaid, reputation-rich sensor network, and because phones now sign captures a two-person team can build the verification layer instead of hardware.
first_30_days: Recruit 30 spotters from ship- and plane-spotting forums in two port cities. Take 10 paid pilot tasks at about $75 from a marine insurance broker or sanctions consultancy, build the verification pipeline around C2PA validation plus AIS cross-checks, and then apply to an SBIR or commercial solutions opening on commercial ground truth.

title: Bereavement Aftercare for Independent Funeral Homes
one_liner: A white-label 13-month aftercare program that funeral homes buy to keep the newly widowed connected after the casseroles stop.
customer: Independent funeral homes (roughly 18,000 in the US, mostly independent), paying $200-350 per family served or a flat monthly fee.
problem: Grief tech money chases griefbots and digital memorials. The real gap is months 2-13, when widowhood drives isolation, depression and elevated mortality. Funeral directors hold the only list of newly bereaved households and a position of trust, but 'aftercare' is usually a brochure and a card. Cremation rates above 60% shrink revenue per call, and independents need loyalty and pre-need referrals to survive against consolidators.
solution: A packaged program: scheduled outreach calls at day 3, 14, 30 and 90, plus first-holiday and anniversary contacts. Small 'second-Thursday' peer groups hosted in the funeral home's own room. A paperwork concierge for Social Security, pensions and accounts, which is the logistics half of grief. A prolonged-grief screener at 6 months with referral to partner clinicians. Software runs scripts, scheduling, facilitator rosters and flags.
why_now: WHO's 2025 framing of loneliness as a measured global health metric gives directors a vocabulary and a reason to act. Rising cremation share squeezes revenue per family. Boomer-parent deaths are rising. Independents are hunting a differentiator against Service Corporation International-style chains.
revenue_model: $200-350 per family served billed to the funeral home, plus referral fees from partner therapists and an uplift in pre-need sales the home can attribute to the program.
non_obvious_insight: Griefbot founders sell to the bereaved at their worst moment. The natural customer for grief is the funeral director, who owns the list, is paid nothing after day 3, and buys aftercare as a marketing and retention expense at his best moment.
first_30_days: Sell 5 funeral homes at $300 per family through state funeral-director association meetings. Hire two part-time facilitators (hospice social workers). Run the first second-Thursday group. Track 6-month contact retention and pre-need referrals as the proof for the next 50 homes.

title: DIC Finder for Veteran Families at Funerals
one_liner: A tool that reads a veteran's death certificate, hospice diagnosis and DD-214 to spot survivor benefits the widow does not know exist, sold to funeral homes and hospices rather than to families.
customer: Funeral homes (roughly 18,000 to 19,000 in the U.S.) that want a differentiated service for veteran families, and hospices with veteran programs. State veteran departments and accredited service officers are downstream partners.
problem: The Vietnam-era generation is now in the last phase of life and forms a large share of veteran deaths. The PACT Act (2022) expanded presumptive conditions for Agent Orange, burn pit and other exposures, so many widows may qualify for Dependency and Indemnity Compensation (DIC, on the order of $1,700 a month, check the current rate). Others may qualify for the Aid and Attendance survivor pension, or accrued benefits. Most never file. The death certificate says 'cardiac arrest' or 'respiratory failure' rather than the underlying service-connected condition. The funeral director's VA paperwork is only for the flag, headstone and burial allowance, and nobody reads the chart for exposure history. The hospice chaplain hears the veteran's service story at the bedside and the widow's money worries at the kitchen table, but has no tool to connect them.
solution: A web and mobile intake tool run at the arrangement conference or at the hospice bereavement visit. It photographs the DD-214, asks a 5-minute exposure and service history (deployment dates and locations, unit, conditions), and matches them against presumptive-condition and location lists. It flags likely DIC, survivor pension and accrued-benefit eligibility, and pre-fills VA Form 21P-534EZ. It then hands the case, with a warm introduction, to an accredited VSO representative or an accredited claims agent. The tool also stores the veteran's story fields so a funeral home can honor the person accurately.
why_now: The PACT Act has created a large wave of newly presumptive conditions, and claim volumes at the VA are at record levels. Vietnam-era veterans are aging into their peak mortality years. As I understand VA rules, accredited representatives can only charge fees after an initial decision, and legislation to tighten fees on predatory claim sharks has been moving. That pushes the sustainable model toward a B2B payer, not families. AI document extraction now makes DD-214 and death-certificate parsing cheap and reliable. Confirm current DIC rates and fee rules before launch.
revenue_model: SaaS for funeral homes at $149 to $299 a month per location, with a per-case add-on for premium processing. Hospices and state veteran departments pay a per-completed-referral fee or a flat annual license. The VSO or accredited-agent partner pays for qualified leads only where the rules allow it, so this must be reviewed by counsel. Families pay nothing.
non_obvious_insight: The money is unclaimed not because widows are lazy but because the trigger event is the funeral, and the only professional in the room (the funeral director) has no financial incentive or training to read a service history. Funeral homes will pay to look like heroes to veteran families, since it feeds pre-need referrals for the next generation, which is where their margin lives.
first_30_days: Partner with one accredited county veteran service officer and two independent funeral homes near a large veteran population. Build the intake as a form plus a manual review by the VSO in week one, before any automation. Run 15 real cases at no charge and record dollars unlocked per family. Use those numbers to close five paying funeral homes at $149 a month. Have a veterans-law attorney review the fee and referral structure before charging anyone.

title: Hotel-Signed Days-in-Country Proofs for Remote Teams
one_liner: Hotels and co-living spaces issue signed, privacy-minimal 'nights in this country' attestations, so employers can prove where remote staff worked without tracking their phones.
customer: Finance, tax or mobility leads at remote-first companies of 30-500 staff that run 'work from anywhere' weeks. Secondary payers are co-living operators and boutique hotels that want a 'workation-verified' badge.
problem: A few weeks abroad can create payroll, social-security and permanent-establishment exposure, and employers need day counts to defend their position. In the EU, GPS or phone tracking of staff is legally toxic (GDPR proportionality, works councils), so companies rely on self-reported spreadsheets. The EU Entry/Exit System has logged border crossings automatically since April 2026, yet neither traveler nor employer gets that data in a usable form. 40+ nomad-visa regimes each have different thresholds.
solution: A thin layer on top of hotel and co-living check-in. At checkout the guest opts in, and the property issues a signed attestation (country, region, date range, licence ID, guest name and nothing else) into the traveler's wallet. The employer's HR or tax tool ingests it by CSV or API, and a country rules pack warns when a threshold is near. The MVP needs no integration: a web form, a signed PDF with a QR code, and a shared ledger template.
why_now: EES has been fully live since 10 Apr 2026, so stays are now machine-tracked at the border but invisible to employers. ETIAS slipping to 2027 keeps the friction alive. Hybrid and workation policies have matured, and 40+ nomad visas make cross-border patchwork the norm.
revenue_model: The employer pays about $6 per attestation or $10 per employee per year for the ledger and rules pack. The property pays about $49 a month for a verified listing in a 'workation-ready' directory. Tax advisers can resell it.
non_obvious_insight: Employers cannot lawfully surveil location, but hospitality already produces third-party presence records by law (guest registration and folios). The missing piece is a consent-based export, so the evidence sits in the hotel and not on the phone.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 co-living spaces and boutique hotels (Lisbon, Canaries, Split, Tbilisi) through operator communities. Have one cross-border tax adviser review a one-page attestation spec. Issue attestations by hand. Pitch 5 remote-first startups through their payroll and tax advisers at a $500 pilot, and count first revenue when the first ledger is delivered.

title: Alt-Data From AI-Training Gig Workers
one_liner: A worker-owned pay-transparency panel for expert data contractors. Its aggregated signals on which domains are hiring, what they pay and how many hours exist become a leading-indicator dataset for investors and rival platforms.
customer: Hedge funds, VCs and AI-lab competitive-intelligence teams pay $30-150k a year for the index. Workers get the basic tier free or for $9-15 a month.
problem: Mercor's reported gross run rate went from about $0.5B to $2B in nine months, and the category claims millions of contractors, yet nobody outside the labs can see which skills are in demand or when a domain saturates. Workers complain of falling pay and have no rate data, while investors price a $10-25B category on anecdotes.
solution: A browser extension plus web app where contractors log, or auto-capture from their own dashboards, pay rate, hours offered, rejections and coarse project category (never confidential content). There is a public 'Levels.fyi for AI gigs' leaderboard by platform and domain, and a paid weekly index of hours availability and pay by domain, with saturation early-warnings.
why_now: The human-data market went from niche to multi-billion in a year, contractors are publicly vocal (HN, Verge, Wired coverage) and investor appetite for AI-adjacent labor data is high. No panel exists.
revenue_model: Institutional data subscriptions ($50-150k a year), a premium worker tier ($9-15 a month) and possibly sponsored placements from challenger platforms recruiting supply.
non_obvious_insight: Gig workers are usually treated as supply, but here they are a sensor network that reads the frontier labs' priorities weeks before any press release. Workers will join because it helps them negotiate and avoid saturated domains. Platforms can't easily object to workers sharing their own pay data, provided the design avoids NDA-covered project details.
first_30_days: Seed 300 members from data-annotation subreddits and Discords with a pay-rate survey. Publish a 'State of expert AI gig pay' report. Pitch 10 funds and 3 VC platform teams a sample weekly index, and land one paid pilot.

title: Human-Backed Login for Senior-Serving Software
one_liner: A drop-in login layer for apps whose users are 65+ that replaces passwords with a two-tap flow, a spoken one-time code by phone call (landline included), family delegates and a live concierge who can walk anyone in.
customer: Vertical SaaS vendors whose users are older adults: senior-living and home-care family portals, community and church software, benefits and Medicare-broker portals, pharmacy and telehealth apps, funeral-planning tools. They pay about $0.80-2 per active senior per month, $3 per concierge-assisted login, with a $299/month minimum.
problem: An operator of a ~10-year-old SaaS used heavily by people 65+ says users 'are tired and frustrated about remembering the domain/path to login screen and then which email/password they used', and that simplification has not fixed it. The 60 responses show what fails: forced resets, masked passwords, magic links (older users struggle switching apps), QR codes and passkeys. What people say they'd pay for is a human: 'elderly individuals want a solution rather than a lesson', and a 'code that you can type in on another device... my grandmother could call and read me a code'.
solution: Per-customer short vanity login URL plus a large 'Call me' button that triggers a phone call reading a short code aloud, working for landlines and flip phones, then persistent trusted-device sessions that effectively never log out. A family-delegate approve/reset flow, no forced password rotation, and no masked fields by default. When automation fails, a live concierge line verifies identity via vendor-supplied challenge questions and completes recovery. Ship as an SDK/widget plus hosted pages, with audit logs suitable for HIPAA-adjacent customers, and report the reduction in login-related support tickets per customer.
why_now: Big platforms pushed passkeys to consumers in 2025-2026 and older users, and the relatives who support them, are loudly reporting confusion and lockouts. The same vendors are under pressure to support MFA. Telephony APIs make voice-delivered codes cheap, and support cost per senior user is the metric operators feel.
revenue_model: Per-active-senior monthly fee, per-assisted-login fee for concierge calls, $299/month minimum, and an annual contract with an ticket-reduction guarantee for larger vendors.
non_obvious_insight: Authentication products optimize against attackers; for the 65+ user the dominant failure is support cost and churn, and the operators in the thread say the answer they would pay for is a human plus a code they can read out loud, not a better protocol. Every fashionable option (passkeys, magic links, QR) was named as failing for this group in the same thread. Evidence: Ask HN 'Easiest UX for Seniors', 58 points, 60 comments https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47729327; passkey confusion for elderly relatives and recovery gaps https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49010448.
first_30_days: Wire Twilio Verify's voice channel to a hosted 'Call me to log in' page and staff a three-person phone shift. Pitch 20 founders of senior-vertical SaaS (found via LinkedIn and association vendor directories), starting with the Ask HN author. Offer a $299/month 60-day pilot that measures login-related support tickets before and after, and convert on a shown reduction.

title: Peak-Load Call Service for Mid-Size Factories
one_liner: Predict the handful of hours a year that set a facility's capacity charge and alert the plant manager to cut load, paid as a share of verified savings.
customer: Commercial and industrial sites of 300 kW to 5 MW in PJM (and ERCOT 4CP) territories that demand-response aggregators ignore: cold storage, water and wastewater plants, plastics and aggregates producers, ice rinks and indoor farms. Energy brokers and consultants are the channel.
problem: A customer's capacity tag (PLC) is set by usage during a few system-peak hours, and its cost then sits on every bill for a year. PJM capacity prices have risen roughly tenfold since 2024/25, with recent auctions clearing at the cap of about $330/MW-day, so a 1 MW site's tag is worth six figures. Owners either never curtail and overpay, or curtail on 20+ hot days and lose production. Aggregators skim 20 to 40% and focus on large accounts.
solution: Model the probability that each upcoming hour ranks in the system's top peaks for the site's zone or utility rules. Use weather ensembles, load forecasts, calendar effects and, critically, the season's running maximum so far. Send a text or BMS signal with the expected value of curtailing against the plant's own curtailment cost. Cut curtailment days from about 25 to about 8 and stop alerting once the peaks have been 'caught'.
why_now: Data-center load growth has pushed PJM capacity clearing prices to the cap two auctions in a row, and those costs are now hitting commercial bills. Open AI weather ensembles (ECMWF AIFS, NOAA) make sharper probabilistic forecasts cheap. The just-finished 2026 summer is fresh evidence for a backtest pitch.
revenue_model: 20 to 25% of verified savings (measured from the next year's PLC change), a $250 to $500 monthly alert subscription, and $2K to $5K paid load audits. Brokers and consultants get a channel rebate.
non_obvious_insight: Quants see 'top 5 hours out of 4,000' as an order-statistics and optimal-stopping problem with asymmetric payoffs, not a pure forecasting problem. As the season's record load rises, the threshold to enter the top 5 becomes known, the option value of alerts collapses, and you can stop curtailing early. Incumbents earn more the more events they call, so their models over-alert. The savings show up a year later on an invoice nobody links to behavior, so customers underinvest without a counterfactual 'what your tag would have been' report.
first_30_days: Use the off-season to pull public PJM hourly load and zonal data, backtest 2019 to 2026 peaks, and generate a free 'what your tag would have been' report for 100 facilities found through EIA and utility-tariff lists. Sell $3K load audits to the first five, sign shared-savings pilots for summer 2027, and recruit two energy brokers as channel partners.

title: The Junior Bench: Rent-a-Resident for AI Review
one_liner: Mid-size accounting, legal and insurance firms rent trained new grads for 12 weeks to verify their AI-produced work, rebuilding the vanished junior rung as a paid residency.
customer: Regional accounting firms, boutique law firms, insurance brokerages and healthcare revenue-cycle companies; new grads join as paid residents.
problem: Employers stopped hiring juniors because AI does the grunt work, yet they still need future seniors. AI-exposed majors have 5 points lower initial employment, grads are 42% underemployed, and 22-25 year-olds in exposed jobs are 19% below trend. Meanwhile firms carry liability for AI-drafted work that nobody is trained to verify well.
solution: A cohort residency. Two weeks of domain and AI-verification training, then about ten weeks embedded in the firm's workflow reviewing AI-drafted workpapers, contract abstracts or claims against sources, with seeded-error scoring. The firm pays a weekly rate and can convert residents to hires. Each resident builds a scored 'verification record' that becomes the credential.
why_now: Payroll data show a widening hiring gap since August 2025. Firms are AI-first but facing quality and liability incidents, and partner pipelines will look empty in about five years.
revenue_model: About $1,800-2,500 per resident-week from the firm against roughly $900-1,100 wage cost, giving 40-50% gross margin. Optional conversion fee if hired early.
non_obvious_insight: AI did not remove the junior job; it turned it from doing into checking. Checking is a trainable, measurable skill with an obvious buyer: the firm that carries the liability for AI errors.
first_30_days: Sell to 3 regional CPA firms ahead of busy season with 5 residents each. Recruit from local accounting grads. Build an error-injection test set to score residents. Charge from week one.

title: Broker Non-Payment Bond-Claim Collective for Small Carriers
one_liner: A service that files carriers' unpaid-load claims against the broker's surety bond and FMCSA record, pools every claimant against the same broker, and publishes a real days-to-pay broker score built from actual payment outcomes.
customer: Small carriers and owner-operators (1 to 10 trucks), including hot-shot and box-truck carriers who don't factor every load. A second revenue stream comes from carriers who pay to check brokers before hauling.
problem: Small unpaid loads are too small for a lawyer and too big to shrug off. One carrier reported a $600 CAD load completed in November 2025 still unpaid in June 2026, after 50+ emails and calls that got only automated replies from a 'Legal Dispute Department'. Their workaround was to 'sign up with factoring companies' who 'either approve or deny'. Meanwhile freight rates have stayed squeezed since 2022, so broker failures and slow payers keep coming.
solution: The carrier uploads the rate confirmation, proof of delivery and invoice. The service verifies the broker's authority and bond or trust-fund status from public FMCSA data, sends a formal demand, and files the claim with the broker's surety (federal rules require property brokers to carry financial security, at $75,000, which is paid out pro rata when many claimants exist). It files an FMCSA complaint and logs every step. The key mechanic is pooling: claims against the same broker are grouped so its claimants are first in line and can cite a pattern. All outcomes feed a broker pay-speed database ('median days to pay', 'claims filed', 'claims paid') that carriers check before booking a load. A trucking attorney reviews templates to stay clear of unauthorized-practice issues.
why_now: The freight recession is still going: the owner-operator thread 'Rates are crashing and fuel to the moon!' began in March 2022 and was on page 1,134 as of Sept 26, 2026. Squeezed brokers pay slowly or fail, and forums are full of fraud and non-payer alerts. Document-heavy claim filing can now be automated cheaply. Factoring companies increasingly reject unknown or slow brokers, which pushes more risk back to unfactored small carriers.
revenue_model: 20 to 25% contingency on recovered amounts. A $15 per month subscription for broker pay-speed lookups and alerts. Later, sell the broker payment-behavior data to factoring companies and load boards.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not the collection letter but the payment-behavior data no credit bureau has, and it is created only by filing claims in bulk. The owner of one 'fraud alert' thread described 50+ emails and only automated replies over 7 months for a $600 CAD load, with a second victim in the same thread and factoring as the only workaround (https://www.thetruckersreport.com/truckingindustryforum/posts/13536421/). The margin squeeze is ongoing: the rates-and-fuel thread reached page 1,134 in Sept 2026 (https://www.thetruckersreport.com/truckingindustryforum/posts/13542683/). A new-authority owner-operator says he cannot get financing and rents a box truck by the day, missing about $4,000 a day in loads, which shows how thin small carriers' cash is (https://www.thetruckersreport.com/truckingindustryforum/posts/13465676/). The bond rule detail is from general knowledge of FMCSA broker financial-security requirements and needs legal confirmation.
first_30_days: Week 1: recruit a trucking attorney to review one claim template. Post in the TruckersReport Freight Broker forum offering free claim filing to carriers in the fraud-alert threads. Weeks 2 to 3: file 15 to 20 claims by hand, group them by broker, and record response times. Week 4: publish the first 'days-to-pay' leaderboard of 25 brokers, and start charging 20% contingency. Target: 30 claims filed and 5 paid, with the leaderboard as the top-of-funnel.

title: Benefits Administrator for Pet-Care Subsidies
one_liner: When hundreds of millions in philanthropy and city funds must reach the right households through thousands of small clinics, someone needs the HSA-administrator equivalent: eligibility, vouchers, payment and audit.
customer: Foundation grantees and programs (Duffield and PetSmart Charities recipients), county animal services and spay-neuter voucher programs. Clinics are the redemption side.
problem: Duffield committed $250M over 5 years, starting with 250 grants of $10K plus $10M in multi-year awards. Grantees run eligibility by paper forms and spreadsheets, clinics wait weeks for reimbursement, funders cannot compare cost per pet outcome, and fraud and overhead eat funds.
solution: Verify proxy eligibility (SNAP, Medicaid, housing-voucher documents or benefit APIs), issue capped QR or card vouchers by procedure category, pay clinics within 5 business days, and export standardized reporting (pets treated, cost, outcome, declined) to funders. Define a shared outcome taxonomy that becomes the field standard.
why_now: The $250M Duffield commitment (2026-09-17) and PetSmart Charities' $100M created hundreds of new grantees at once. Card-issuing and instant-payout APIs let a small team run a closed-loop voucher program.
revenue_model: 4-7% administration fee on disbursed dollars (funded from grant overhead lines), SaaS fee per grantee, and data and reporting subscriptions for funders.
non_obvious_insight: Money is not the binding constraint; distribution rails are. Human benefit administrators (HSA and EBT processors) became large businesses because funders needed accountability. About 250 first-round grantees have no back office, so the standard-setter for outcomes measurement owns the funders' reporting.
first_30_days: Contact 20 first-round grantees and 5 county animal services. Offer a free voucher tool to one program with a $10K grant, run through 3 clinics, and publish an outcomes one-pager. Then brief funder program officers on standardized reporting.

title: Hours Wallet for Medicaid Work Requirements
one_liner: A text-first tool that proves 80 hours or $580 a month of work for gig and cash earners, paid by Medicaid plans and clinics that lose money when members drop off.
customer: Payers: Medicaid managed-care plans, FQHCs and hospital financial-counseling teams paying per enrolled or retained member. Users: adults 19-64 in the Medicaid expansion group with irregular income (gig, seasonal, cash, self-employed).
problem: The CMS interim final rule (June 1, 2026) requires about 43 states plus DC to enforce 80 hours per month of work, service or school, or at least $580 per month of earnings, by January 1, 2027, at application and renewal. If compliance cannot be verified the person gets only 30 calendar days to prove it. Proof means pay stubs and letters from employers or volunteer organizations. Arkansas's 2018 requirement cost 18,000 people coverage for failing to meet work or reporting rules.
solution: SMS or WhatsApp-first app that (a) connects gig-platform exports or bank deposits to test the $580 income alternative, (b) sends one-tap timestamped attestation links to a boss, food-bank coordinator or volunteer supervisor, (c) auto-formats the state's monthly report and files it, (d) alerts the member before the 30-day cure window closes, and (e) screens for exemptions such as parents or caretakers of children under 14 and disability. It gives the payer a dashboard of at-risk members.
why_now: The federal rule is final as of June 2026 and states must be live by January 1, 2027 (some earlier, with Nebraska reportedly starting May 1, 2026). Self-attestation is only allowed for 2027, after which documentation is required, so 2027 is the last cheap window to build a member base and data habit before documentation hardens.
revenue_model: Per-member-per-month or success fee per retained member from MCOs and FQHCs (about $3-$10/member/month or a bounty per successful renewal), with a free tier for members; secondary revenue from employer-attestation seats for staffing and home-care agencies.
non_obvious_insight: States must first use payroll and other data to verify compliance, which leaves the residual, hardest population (cash, gig and self-employed workers) exactly where a proof tool is needed. Payers, not members, have the money, because each lost member is lost capitation revenue. The CMS rule text (https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/medicaid-community-engagement-requirement-certain-individuals-interim-final-rule-comment-period-cms) gives the $580 alternative, 30-day cure period and exemptions, and KFF's data brief cites the 18,000 Arkansas coverage losses (https://www.kff.org/medicaid/issue-brief/understanding-the-intersection-of-medicaid-and-work-what-does-the-data-say/). Reddit was unreachable, so the r/personalfinance and r/legaladvice 'how do I prove my hours?' demand is forecast from the rule and explainers rather than quoted threads.
first_30_days: Build the $580 income test and attestation-link flow for Nebraska (reportedly already live) plus one January 2027 state. Approach 2 FQHCs and one regional MCO or hospital financial counseling team for a free pilot, and give the tool free to food banks and legal-aid groups as distribution. Aim for 200 pilot members, then convert the clinics to a per-member fee with retained-coverage data as the proof.

title: Farm Income Dial: ACA Cliff Management
one_liner: A December planning service that uses the grain-contract and input-prepay levers farmers already control to keep household income under the 400% poverty cliff and avoid repaying a full year of health subsidies.
customer: Farm families who buy ACA marketplace coverage. KFF estimates about 27% of farmers do, nearly triple the adult average. The co-op grain desks and rural CPA firms that advise them pay for a white-label version.
problem: The enhanced ACA subsidies expired on December 31, 2025, so the hard cutoff at 400% of poverty is back (roughly $130k for a family of four). The 2025 tax law also removed repayment caps for tax year 2026. A farm family that projected income under the line and then lands $2,000 over must repay every dollar of advance credits, often $15k to $25k. Farm income is lumpy and depends on prices and yields nobody knows in January. Farm CPAs optimize the federal tax bracket, not the ACA cliff, and nobody connects the two.
solution: Farmers connect their grain settlements, deferred contracts, prepaid inputs and equipment purchases. The tool tracks estimated 2026 MAGI against the cliff and gives a concrete action list: how many bushels to defer into 2027, how much fertilizer to prepay, when to elect CCC loan treatment, when to buy equipment. It also models plan choice for 2027 open enrollment, including Farm Bureau non-ACA plans and their underwriting risks. Every recommendation is reviewed by the household's CPA, so this is planning software and not tax advice.
why_now: This is the first tax year with no repayment cap and no enhanced credits. Marketplace enrollment fell from 22.1M to 19.2M in a year. The planning window closes December 31, 2026, and every Iowa farm family on a marketplace plan is exposed right now.
revenue_model: $350 to $600 per farm household per season. Broker commissions from carriers when the tool places 2027 coverage. White-label licenses to rural CPA firms and co-op grain desks ($50 to $100 per client). Optional success fee of 10% of the protected credit.
non_obvious_insight: The ACA cliff is controlled with the same pen that signs deferred-payment contracts. The co-op grain desk is the real MAGI control panel for farm families. CPAs do not see it because they only meet clients in February, after the levers are gone.
first_30_days: Partner with 2 rural CPA firms and one co-op grain desk. Build a spreadsheet-grade calculator plus a one-page 'cliff letter' for clients. Run a 'Cliff Night' at the co-op with farm families in October and November. Convert 30 to 50 households at $350 before the December deadline and document dollars saved.

title: Childcare Credits Instead of Builder Rate Buydowns
one_liner: Homebuilders replace temporary mortgage rate buydowns with redeemable childcare credits, and the program builds the licensed care space inside the community.
customer: Small and mid-size spec and production builders with unsold inventory in family-heavy exurbs (Sunbelt and Midwest), and master-planned community developers. The end buyers are young families with kids under 5.
problem: 63% of builders use incentives and 80-90% of new-home sales need rate buydowns with 30-year rates near 7%, yet completions fell 27.1% year over year. Buydowns are a one-time cost that fades in 2-3 years. For a household with toddlers, childcare ($13,128 per child, more than a mortgage for two kids in 45 states) is the actual affordability wall, and new suburbs are childcare deserts.
solution: The builder funds a Family Care Credit (for example $400 a month for 24 months) redeemable only at licensed providers in a vetted network. The startup pre-commits reserved occupancy with providers and helps a provider open in the community, using a builder-built care-ready clubhouse room, flex unit or model home at cost. The credit's cost accrues only when used, so expected builder spend can undercut a $12-20K buydown. Marketing kit: 'move-in ready, childcare included'.
why_now: Incentives are at a cyclical high, starts are steady but completions fell 27.1% and builders are financing shops. ROAD to Housing Act streamlining for small multifamily and factory-built homes aims at exactly these family starter products. Dependent-care FSA limits rose to $7,500, and childcare deserts are politically salient.
revenue_model: 10-15% program fee on credit dollars funded by the builder, per-family placement fee from providers, and later a margin on prepaid-slot financing.
non_obvious_insight: Builders see incentives as price cuts, but a family with a toddler values $400 a month of childcare more than a temporary rate cut. A builder is already a construction company, so converting a room to licensed space costs them little and is worth a rent-free facility to a provider. The guaranteed occupancy is what makes the provider's economics work in the first place.
first_30_days: Target five small builders with spec inventory in fast-growing exurbs. Check local childcare deserts with the CAP map, sign one builder for a 10-home pilot, and line up two licensed home providers. Launch a 'move-in ready with childcare' landing page and compare lead conversion to the builder's buydown ads. Have counsel confirm the credit's treatment against buyer-concession rules.

title: Vendor Exit Desk for Fleets and Contractors
one_liner: A contingency-fee service that gets small fleets and home-service contractors out of predatory software and telematics contracts, and recovers the money the vendors keep billing.
customer: Owner-operators and fleets of 5-200 trucks locked into telematics or ELD contracts (Samsara, Motive). Also HVAC, plumbing and electrical contractors on ServiceTitan, Housecall Pro or Jobber, and small property managers on AppFolio. The owner or office manager pays, and only out of money recovered or saved.
problem: These vendors sell month-to-month or 1-year terms, then enforce hidden multi-year renewals, exit fees, ship-date billing and auto-renew windows. Support is now AI-only, so the customer cannot reach a human who can fix it. One Samsara reviewer was charged $29,000 for a 3-year contract after negotiating 1 year. Another lost about $32,000 paying for unused devices for 1 year and 9 months. ServiceTitan customers report quoted exit fees of $22,000, $29,000 and $37,000. An AppFolio reviewer was billed a $1,290 cancellation fee and said cancelling took 4 months.
solution: The customer forwards the contract and 3 recent invoices. The service does six things. (1) Extract renewal dates and notice windows, then send certified-mail non-renewal notices on the right day. (2) Audit billing against reality: billing that started at ship date rather than install date, decommissioned trucks still billed, duplicate accounts, and charges after cancellation. (3) Build a dispute packet with the sales promises, the timeline, and a card-network chargeback filing where the payment was on a business card. (4) Negotiate with the vendor's retention or legal team, with a partner attorney handling demand letters so the desk does not practice law itself. (5) Handle the data export. (6) Refer the customer to a replacement vendor that pays a bounty for the switch.
why_now: The 1-2 star reviews are dated 2026. They show vendors under public-market pressure enforcing renewals and paywalling features, for example Samsara charging $10 per truck for a feature shown in the demo. They also show support moving to AI. A Housecall Pro review dated Sept 28, 2026 says 'No support unless you want to speak with AI', and a Tithe.ly reviewer says the same in Feb 2026. Customers have nobody to call, so a human escalation path is now something they will pay for.
revenue_model: 25-30% of recovered or avoided dollars, with no fee if nothing is recovered. A $199 flat billing audit for small accounts. A $300-$1,000 referral bounty from the competing vendor that wins each switched fleet or contractor. An optional $29 per vendor per year renewal-watch subscription.
non_obvious_insight: The leads identify themselves. Each reviewer posts the vendor, the dollar amount, the date and the grievance publicly, so the whole first-year pipeline is already listed. Evidence: Samsara ($29,000 3-year contract, $32,000 unused devices, $900/month billed from ship date, $10/truck feature paywall) at https://www.trustpilot.com/review/samsara.com. ServiceTitan ($22K, $29K and $37K exit quotes) at https://www.trustpilot.com/review/servicetitan.com. Motive (renewal-window traps, charged again after cancelling) at https://www.trustpilot.com/review/gomotive.com. AppFolio ($1,290 fee, 4-month cancellation) at https://www.trustpilot.com/review/appfolio.com. Housecall Pro (charged $189 three times after cancelling, price doubled from $351 to $681) at https://www.trustpilot.com/review/housecallpro.com. The winning product is not software. It is a library of each vendor's contract clauses, notice windows and escalation paths, built up case by case, and it gets more effective with every dispute settled.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: pull the roughly 300 public 1-2 star reviews from the last 12 months across those 5 vendors and tag each by vendor, dollar amount and whether the customer is still active. Days 8-14: contact reviewers by the review reply or an email lookup, offering a free contract read. Sign a contract attorney on a small retainer. Days 15-30: take 5-10 contingency cases and publish 'how to cancel [vendor]' pages, since people search that phrase. Use the settled cases to build the clause library. Also pitch 2 competing telematics vendors on the switch bounty.

title: Trusted Firmware for Chinese-Made Robots
one_liner: A security-audited, network-isolated software and attestation layer that lets US labs, utilities and cities legally buy and run cheap Unitree-class robots.
customer: US universities and research labs, utilities, municipal fleets, critical-infrastructure operators, and integrators reselling Chinese quadrupeds and humanoids.
problem: Chinese makers hold 86% of humanoid shipments and their robots cost a fraction of US alternatives, but security teams block procurement over cloud telemetry, remote access and radio vulnerabilities disclosed in 2025. There is no neutral, certified 'clean' stack, and barriers are going up.
solution: A replacement software stack and wrapper: local-only operation, cloud services removed, wireless interfaces locked down, signed OTA updates under customer keys, an SBOM, and a continuous-audit attestation report that security auditors accept. Add an optional network-quarantine gateway appliance.
why_now: Tariffs, the FCC's DJI action and expected legislation are tightening. Unitree's IPO signals the supply will keep coming, so buyers with budgets are stuck between the price advantage and compliance.
revenue_model: $500-1,500 per robot a year for the license and updates, $10-30k per security assessment, and about $800 per gateway appliance.
non_obvious_insight: Each time the US restricts a Chinese hardware category, a trust layer becomes the only route for legal buyers. Everyone bets on which hardware wins, but the money sits in the compliance gap. Risk: an outright ban would kill the market, so design for a pivot to open-source or allied hardware.
first_30_days: Buy a Go2 and a G1, reproduce the publicly documented vulnerabilities, and publish a hardening guide. Offer free audits to 5 university robotics labs' IT security officers and convert 3 to paid assessments at $10-15k.

title: Post-Montgomery Walk-Around Audits for Freight Brokers
one_liner: A gig network of working and retired truckers who physically inspect the carriers a broker hires and hand back a lawyer-ready diligence file.
customer: Mid-size freight brokers and 3PLs ($50M to $1B gross bookings, 10 to 200 staff). The budget owner is the VP of compliance/risk or general counsel. Secondary buyers are contingent-auto and broker E&O underwriters, and shippers that run in-house brokerage.
problem: On May 14, 2026 the Supreme Court unanimously held in Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II that negligent-selection suits against brokers are not preempted by federal law. Brokers now have to prove they exercised reasonable care picking a carrier. Their vetting is entirely digital: SAFER lookups, insurance certificates, ID checks. Nobody has ever looked at the yard. Chameleon carriers with clean paperwork, fake addresses and fictitious pickups sail through, and so do genuinely dangerous small fleets. Verisk CargoNet put Q2 2026 theft losses at $304.6M, more than double Q2 2025, even though incident counts fell.
solution: Book a 45-minute physical walk-around of a carrier's listed terminal, yard or the driver's truck for $175 to $350. The trucker follows a 40-point protocol and shoots geo-stamped photo and video: steer tire tread and sidewall damage, brake chamber stroke, lights, ELD present and working, trailer age and VIN against registration, whether the address has a shop, lot and signage, and a two-minute driver interview. The broker gets a scored, reproducible report filed against the carrier ID. Upsells are a quarterly re-walk for top-tier carriers on high-risk lanes, and 'eyes on pickup', where a local trucker sits at the shipper's dock and confirms the right driver and truck load the freight (aimed at high-value copper, electronics and pharma loads). Build the checklist with a trucking-defense attorney so it holds up as evidence.
why_now: The May 2026 Montgomery ruling created a brand-new legal duty and every broker general counsel is scrambling. Insurers are repricing broker liability. Fictitious-pickup and impersonation theft keeps growing (Verisk CargoNet counted 158 fictitious pickups in Q2 2026). Meanwhile English-proficiency out-of-service enforcement and the February 2026 non-domiciled CDL rule are churning the small-carrier population, so more unknown carriers are entering the market.
revenue_model: Per-audit fees of $175 to $350, with the trucker keeping about 45 to 55%. Annual diligence-program retainers of $25k to $100k for brokers that want a defined audit cadence. Insurer premium-credit revenue share. A recurring data subscription selling carrier physical-condition scores back to the wider broker market.
non_obvious_insight: Any 20-year driver can size up a carrier's yard in 90 seconds. Chameleon outfits have one shiny truck, no shop, mismatched trailers, cords showing on the steer tires, and drivers who can't name their dispatcher. Digital vetting checks paperwork; a jury after Montgomery will ask 'did anyone actually look?' The product isn't a tool, it's discoverable proof of reasonable care. Drivers are already within 30 miles of nearly any carrier and sit idle on 34-hour restarts and at detention, so the inspector supply is cheaper and more credible than any consultancy's.
first_30_days: Recruit 15 vetted current and retired drivers from CDL forums and trucker Facebook groups and pay them per audit. Pay a trucking-defense attorney $2k to $3k to co-design the checklist and co-brand a 'Montgomery diligence protocol'. Build the capture app as a PWA with forms, geotagged photos and an auto-generated PDF. Cold-email 40 mid-size broker GCs and compliance heads, offering 5 pilot audits at $99 on their riskiest tier-3 carriers. Target 3 paying brokers by day 30 and 100 audits by month 3.

title: Reusable Trust Passport for Bio-AI Access
one_liner: One neutral, portable verification that a biotech or academic lab is legitimate, bound to that lab's agent keys, so frontier AI vendors and DNA/reagent suppliers can accept its agent-placed orders without repeating the diligence.
customer: Small and mid-size biotechs, academic labs and CROs that need relaxed AI safeguards and want agents to order DNA, oligos and reagents. Secondary payers are AI vendors and suppliers who pay per verified check.
problem: On September 17, 2026 Anthropic launched its Life Sciences Verification Program (credential, security and ethics-oversight review, 30-day data retention) and expected hundreds of organizations in week one. Other AI providers, DNA synthesis vendors and cloud labs will each build their own version. Small labs lack SOC 2-style security paperwork, organized IBC documentation or an ethics-oversight file, so they queue or get denied. Machine identities already outnumber humans about 109 to 1 and there is no shared 'know your agent' standard for bio orders.
solution: A one-time dossier (organization identity, IBC/IACUC registration, named biosafety officer, lightweight security review, data-handling policy) issued as a verifiable credential tied to the lab's agent keys. AI vendors and suppliers accept it for access tiers and agent-placed orders, and the credential is continuously monitored and revoked if an IBC approval lapses. Include a readiness checklist and concierge help to complete the paperwork.
why_now: Verification programs started in September 2026, creating an immediate backlog and duplicative-paperwork problem. Agent-order volume is growing, and synthesis-screening rules and frontier-lab safeguards are tightening at the same time.
revenue_model: Flat verification fee ($1.5-5K one-time plus annual renewal), per-check fees from vendors and AI providers, and an enterprise tier for CRO networks and shared core facilities.
non_obvious_insight: Frontier labs cannot be each other's trust anchor, which is why an accredited third-party reviewer that several of them accept is valuable. This is the Vanta/Plaid pattern applied to bio access, and the first concierge revenue comes from the backlog, before any network effect exists.
first_30_days: Build the 'verification readiness' checklist and offer a $2.5K flat concierge service to the first 20 labs that applied. Talk to 3 mid-tier DNA/oligo vendors and 2 cloud labs about accepting your dossier for agent orders. Publish an open template so vendors see you as the standards-setter, then charge for review and monitoring.

title: Get Paid to Care: Family Caregiver Enrollment
one_liner: A navigator that gets family caregivers onto Medicaid and VA payrolls, then becomes the fiscal intermediary that pays them.
customer: Adult children and spouses (45-70) giving 20+ hours a week of unpaid care to a low-income parent or veteran. Secondary buyers are Area Agencies on Aging, Medicaid managed-care plans and state Medicaid agencies that pay fiscal-intermediary fees.
problem: 59M family caregivers gave 49.5B unpaid hours in 2024 (about $1T) and lose roughly $21k a year in income. Every state has Medicaid self-direction, many pay relatives, and the VA has Veteran-Directed Care. But the rules differ by state, the assessment sets the hours, and agencies and fiscal intermediaries earn more by placing an outside aide.
solution: Phase 1 is a state-by-state 'can I get paid?' screener plus done-with-you enrollment: eligibility, application packet, coaching for the nurse assessment (which sets hours), employee onboarding, timesheet and electronic-visit-verification coaching, and appeals. Phase 2 is to become a licensed fiscal intermediary (payroll, background checks, EVV) in states that allow several vendors, and to bill the state a monthly per-participant fee.
why_now: About $911B in federal Medicaid cuts plus work requirements, 41 states with HCBS waitlists over 600k people (average wait 15 months), and Wisconsin agencies 'not able to take new clients' after the 2026 visa and TPS shocks. States now have to lean on the caregiver already in the house.
revenue_model: Families pay a flat $349-499 per successful enrollment, or a lower fee plus a first-year success fee. Phase 2 adds state or MCO fiscal-intermediary per-member-per-month fees. AAAs can pay for referral-sourced enrollment.
non_obvious_insight: The shortage is partly a payment-eligibility problem, not a bodies problem. The gatekeepers who could help families avoid agencies are the agencies and legacy fiscal intermediaries, so no one with a business incentive teaches families the paid-relative pathway.
first_30_days: Pick two states where relatives can be paid and enrollment is open (California's IHSS is the obvious one). Publish the screener and state guides, then capture leads through caregiver support groups, Facebook groups and elder-law firms. Sell a $349 concierge enrollment to the first 20 families and measure approval rate and approved hours.

title: Insured Filing Clerk for Multi-City Contractor Licenses
one_liner: A computer-use agent that renews and files contractor and business licenses across city and county portals that have no APIs, backed by a penalty warranty.
customer: Trade contractors (electricians, plumbers, HVAC, roofers, landscapers, painters), mobile groomers, food trucks and short-term-rental hosts working across many cities or counties, with 2-30 employees.
problem: Each city and county has its own business-license, registration and permit portal, fee schedule and renewal date, with COI and bond uploads. Missing one triggers fines or stop-work orders. Enterprise-priced compliance vendors ignore small firms, and payroll vendors are bundling only payroll compliance (Gusto bought Mosey in April 2026).
solution: An agent operates the same portals a human would to renew, upload COIs and bonds, pay fees with a virtual card and capture receipts. Human reviewers verify sensitive steps. A warranty pays penalties for missed or incorrect filings. Every filing improves a jurisdiction knowledge base of forms, fees and quirks.
why_now: Browser and computer-use agents crossed a reliability threshold in 2025-26, and payroll compliance has been productized, leaving licenses and permits as the untouched adjacent layer.
revenue_model: $59/month plus $15 per filing plus fee pass-through, with the warranty cost built into pricing.
non_obvious_insight: With roughly 19,000 municipalities, no API strategy will ever cover the map, but an agent that uses the human interface can. The moat is the jurisdiction graph and the warranty.
first_30_days: Pick a dense metro cluster with many cities and one trade. Assist 20 contractors with renewals, recording each portal flow, and sign a COI and bond partner for bulk uploads. Track error rate and hours saved.
